KFUPM · IMR — hybrid physics + ML digital twin

Quantitative Unbalance Digital Twin of a Bently Nevada RK-4 Rotor

A physics-informed machine-learning twin that estimates rotor unbalance in engineering units (g·mm, keyphasor phase, per-disk) from live proximity-probe data — and beats both the classical influence-coefficient method and pure ML on the same held-out conditions.

Three twins, one signal chain

The same keyphasor order-tracking front end feeds three inverse models. The hybrid hands the physics estimate to the learner as a prior, so the model corrects the physics residual instead of regressing from scratch — anchoring scale and phase while cleaning up the sub-critical conditioning and rotor-anisotropy bias.

Validation figures

Blind validation — 10 unsealed conditions, unbiased

All ten acquired blind conditions were unsealed after prediction: five balanced (empty disks) and five loaded two-plane cases (some off-grid, some out of the mostly single-disk training range). The models never saw them. This is the honest accuracy figure — and it shows a real trade-off.

Take-away: the learned twins win detection & specificity (no false alarms on balanced rotors); the linear physics wins magnitude on large out-of-distribution two-plane loads (the trees don't extrapolate). Adding two-plane conditions to training is the concrete next step — the hybrid frame already carries the physics scale as a prior.

Method & rigor

Slow-roll runoutcorrected 60–70% of low-speed 1X is runout; subtracted a 251-rpm complex reference per sensor.
Whirl-sensecalibrated Measured phase conjugated to the mounting-angle sense (fixes ±90° flips).
Leakage-free CVenforced GroupKFold on condition_id — repeats/mounts never straddle folds; the three calibration conditions are excluded from every method's score.
2-plane conditioningcharacterized cond(A) ≈ 16.99 (N1) / 24.81 (N2): sub-critical, both disks drive near-rigid motion. This is the localization limiter the hybrid attacks.
Uncertaintyquantified Tree-ensemble spread → per-estimate σ (g·mm), calibrated against held-out error.
